acquisition.why: The demonstrated method (scraped numbers plus ringless voicemail) is not safe under UK PECR/TPS, and many UK trades are sole traders who cannot be cold-emailed or texted. That leaves cold email to limited-company trades, Meta ads to trades (no sale proven) and SEO, which face heavy competition. Agents can run ads and email, but conversion likely needs a demo or call [E].

onboarding.why: Each client needs a UK number, call-forwarding set up on their own mobile or network (voicemail must be off, which they often get wrong), UK SMS sender registration and a trade-specific prompt or link. Some client hand-holding is needed every time [E].

delivery.why: Once configured, GoHighLevel or Twilio workflows send the text and the AI qualifies the lead unattended. Replying to an inbound caller is not cold marketing.

billing.why: Monthly Stripe or GHL SaaS-mode subscription.

support.why: Forwarding breaks, missed texts and bad AI answers to urgent jobs reach the owner directly, and those tradespeople expect a human [E].

scores.R_why: Technically trivial for Ricardo. However, GHL costs about $97-297/month, which eats a £300 test in 1-3 months [E]. Selling to UK tradespeople usually means calls and demos he has no hours for. No sale was closed in the source.
scores.M_why: Heavily commoditised. VoIP providers, Tradify-type job apps, GHL resellers and AI receptionists (e.g. Trillet-style, Rosie) already offer it, and many UK trades rely on WhatsApp Business auto-replies [E].
scores.one_line: Easy to build and runs itself once live, but UK-legal acquisition of tradespeople is hard and the product is a saturated GHL commodity. Weak fit for an agent-run, hands-off business [E].

acquisition.why: Value-first posting in Facebook groups needs a genuine human presence. UK cheer is a tiny niche. App-store and SEO inbound is possible but low-volume [E].

onboarding.why: Self-serve signup and parent import. Parent and child data requires consent capture flows.

delivery.why: Unattended software. Push, email or WhatsApp links avoid SMS consent and cost issues.

support.why: Low-touch with an agent-handled help desk. GDPR and child-data queries are occasional.

scores.R_why: Easily vibe-coded within his hours and budget. However, UK youth cheer is very small; widening to all UK youth sports runs straight into free incumbents. Children's data adds GDPR care.
scores.M_why: Spond (free and dominant in UK grassroots sport), TeamSnap, Heja, Pitchero and plain WhatsApp groups already do this for free. A £5/month single feature has almost no room [E].
scores.one_line: A purely illustrative teaching example with no revenue. Highly automatable, but the UK market is tiny and free tools like Spond already cover it, so it is unattractive.

acquisition.why: Most UK charities are incorporated (CLG or CIO), so cold email is broadly OK, and there is charity-sector SEO and content. However, trust-based sales to trustees are slow, and some smaller unincorporated charities fall outside the corporate exemption [E].

onboarding.why: Each client needs a human-reviewed intake of governance documents, accounts, impact data and project budgets.

delivery.why: Agents can match funders and draft bids, but a human review before submission is essential for quality and accuracy.

billing.why: Retainers can be on Stripe, but success fees depend on award outcomes with months of lag and need manual invoicing and tracking.

support.why: Clients expect a named bid writer and revisions, and funder feedback loops are human.

scores.R_why: Ricardo can build it. The large UK funder landscape (360Giving open data) is a plus. However, the Chartered Institute of Fundraising code discourages commission or success fees, and bid quality needs domain expertise he likely lacks. Review time competes with his 6-8 hours/week.
scores.M_why: Crowded: Grantable, Instrumentl, Plinth and other UK AI bid tools, Funds Online and GrantFinder databases, and charities using ChatGPT directly. Funders are also increasingly wary of AI-drafted bids [E].
scores.one_line: A real UK need with a specific first-hand price claim. However, it is human-review-heavy, success fees conflict with UK fundraising norms, and AI substitutes are commoditising it.

acquisition.why: Most UK bodyshops are limited companies, so cold email is OK, and Meta ads are agent-runnable. Conversion probably needs a demo [E].

onboarding.why: Each shop needs a branded setup, customer-notification consent and integration with, or habit change in, their job workflow.

delivery.why: The software is automated, but status accuracy depends on shop staff updating it unless it is integrated with their management system.

billing.why: Monthly subscription via Stripe or GHL.

support.why: Staff adoption issues and customer complaints about wrong statuses need hands-on help [E].

scores.R_why: Buildable with cheap tooling. However, UK bodyshop work is largely insurer- or accident-management-directed, and those insurer portals and existing bodyshop systems already push status updates. Selling to garages takes calls and visits he has no hours for [E].
scores.M_why: Vertical DMS and estimating platforms (e.g. Bodyshop Manager-type tools, insurer repair-tracking portals) bundle this, so a standalone white-labelled GHL tracker is easy to displace [E].
scores.one_line: A second-hand, single-mention example with no pricing. B2B cold email is legal, but adoption friction and bundled incumbents make it a poor agent-run bet.

acquisition.why: Inbound via content, SEO and the Chrome Web Store is feasible but platform-dependent, and buyers are sceptical of protection claims.

onboarding.why: Self-serve upload, plugin install or API.

delivery.why: Requires R&D-grade adversarial audio and detection. Effectiveness is unproven and decays as new models appear, so it needs ongoing expert work rather than unattended software [E].

support.why: False positives and negatives and 'it got cloned anyway' disputes need careful human handling.

scores.R_why: This is ML-research territory in an arms race, far beyond 6-8 hours/week and £300. Overstated protection claims carry ASA and consumer-law risk, and voice biometrics trigger UK GDPR special-category rules.
scores.M_why: Real and growing demand, but contested by well-funded players: Reality Defender, Resemble, Pindrop, C2PA and Content Credentials from Adobe and Google, and platform-native labels [E].
scores.one_line: A speculative trend observation with no revenue evidence. It needs deep R&D and competes with funded incumbents, so it is not viable for a part-time agent-run test.

acquisition.why: The antique-centre booth provides passive foot traffic, an inbound retail placement, but sales depend on that single location.

onboarding.why: No customer onboarding: shoppers simply buy.

delivery.why: Physical sourcing at 5am car boots, plus pricing, transport and booth stocking, all require a human every time.

billing.why: The centre usually handles the till and pays out monthly minus commission.

support.why: Minimal, but returns and queries go through centre staff and the stock owner.

scores.R_why: Early weekend car-boot runs clash with toddler care, and stall rent (about £80-250/month [E]) plus stock quickly exceed £300. Zero agent leverage.
scores.M_why: UK car boots and antique centres are an established, competitive hobby market with eBay and Vinted price transparency. There is no saturation crisis, but margins are thin [E].
scores.one_line: A purely physical hobby-reselling business with no claims backing it. The computed evidence score is inflated, and nothing here can be agent-run.

acquisition.why: UK pond and dredging contractors are often sole traders, so cold email is restricted. Small Ltd firms and inbound SEO are possible but the niche is tiny.

onboarding.why: Self-serve purchase of lead lists by region is possible.

delivery.why: Agents can map ponds from OS/Environment Agency/OpenStreetMap data, but 'need signals' and accuracy are weak and need human QA.

support.why: Agents handle bad-lead complaints and refunds.

scores.R_why: The UK pond market is a fraction of the 800,000 Texas ponds cited. Landowner personal data needs a UK GDPR lawful basis, and contractors using the leads for cold outreach to farmers face PECR limits.
scores.M_why: Very small buyer pool, unproven demand and easily replicated data, so there is little headroom in the UK [E].
scores.one_line: A US-specific, unproven agent demo. The UK market is tiny and legally awkward on data and outreach, so it should be passed over.

acquisition.why: Paid Meta and Google ads, Amazon KDP and SEO are agent-manageable. However, Meta restricts 'personal hardship' targeting and the source's CAC only broke even, so it is platform-dependent.

delivery.why: Digital ebook or KDP print-on-demand avoids holding inventory, though a higher-ticket back-end programme or community needs some moderation.

billing.why: Stripe or funnel checkout, including order bumps.

support.why: Agents handle refunds and access issues. Distressed customers and legal-adjacent questions need careful escalation.

scores.R_why: The content needs a full rewrite for UK law (no-fault divorce since 2022, separate Scottish law) and to avoid regulated legal advice. A £300 ad budget is only about 3 days at the source's spend, with break-even CAC, so profit depends on unproven upsells [E].
scores.M_why: Amazon has many divorce books, free gov.uk and Citizens Advice guidance exists, and AI chat substitutes are common. Meta ad restrictions add platform risk [E].
scores.one_line: A candid, specific, first-hand single source (break-even CAC, about $5-6k in sales). The funnel is very automatable, but thin margins, UK legal localisation and ad-policy risk make it marginal on £300.
